title: The Sacrifice of the New Creation - 5

content:
As we have studied the offerings of Numbers 15, one phrase has appeared again and again. Over and over Yahweh calls these offerings "a pleasing aroma to Yahweh." Today let us consider what this beautiful phrase really means, and then let us look at another wonderful truth in this same chapter, that there was to be one law for the native-born Israelite and for the foreigner alike. Both of these carry a rich lesson for us, the New Creation.

First, we must be careful to understand what the phrase "a pleasing aroma" does not mean. It does not mean that Yahweh needed the physical smell of a sacrifice, or that He somehow enjoyed the scent of burning flesh and grain the way a hungry man enjoys the smell of food. Yahweh is not fed by our offerings, and He does not depend on anything we bring. Rather, this phrase signifies acceptance. When Scripture says that an offering was a pleasing aroma to Yahweh, it means that the worship offered in obedience to His command was received and accepted by Him. It was pleasing because it came from a heart that honoured Him and obeyed His word. The pleasing aroma was never really about the smell rising from the altar. It was about the obedience rising from the heart.

It is beautiful to see that Christ Himself is described in exactly this way.

Paul writes that Christ "loved us and offered himself as a sacrifice for us, a pleasing aroma to God" (Ephesians 5:2). The offering of Christ upon the cross was the truest and most perfect pleasing aroma that ever rose before the Father. It was the one offering in which the Father found complete and perfect delight. And this leads us to a truth we must hold very carefully, for it guards us against a serious error. Our offerings of fine flour, of oil, and of wine only become a pleasing aroma when they are joined to the sacrifice itself. In the offerings of Numbers 15, the flour and oil and wine never stood alone. They always accompanied the animal, the sacrifice. The grain offering was never presented by itself as though it could please God on its own. It was always brought together with the sacrifice.
This teaches us something we must never forget. Our character, pictured in the fine flour, our Spirit-filled life, pictured in the oil, and our surrendered life, pictured in the poured-out wine, mean nothing at all apart from union with the sacrifice of Christ. If we could somehow bring the finest character, the most Spirit-filled life, and the most complete surrender, and yet bring it apart from Christ, it would not be a pleasing aroma to God. It would be a grain offering with no sacrifice, and Yahweh never commanded such a thing. This guards us against every thought that our own works could please God on their own.

We are not accepted because of the fineness of our flour. We are accepted because our flour is joined to the sacrifice of Christ. He is the offering; we bring only that which accompanies Him. All our devotion becomes acceptable only because it rises together with His one perfect sacrifice. Take away the sacrifice, and the flour is only flour. Join it to Christ, and it becomes a pleasing aroma to God.
Now let us turn to the second truth. In this same chapter, Yahweh declared that these instructions applied not only to the native-born Israelite, but also to the foreigner who lived among them. He said there was to be one law and one ordinance for the Israelite and for the stranger alike. There was not to be one way of approaching God for the Jew and a different way for the foreigner.

All who came before Yahweh were to come according to the same instruction, bringing the same offerings, in the same way. This revealed the justice and the impartiality of God, and it also pointed forward to something greater that would come in the Gospel Age.

For in Christ, the old distinction between Jew and Gentile has been removed. Paul writes that in Christ "There is no longer Jew or Gentile... For you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). And he explains how this happened, saying of Christ, "For he himself has brought peace to us. He united Jews and Gentiles into one people when, in his own body on the cross, he broke down the wall of hostility that separated us" (Ephesians 2:14). Under the Law there had been a middle wall of partition, a real barrier that kept the Gentile at a distance. But the sacrifice of Christ tore that wall down. Now there is one sacrifice, and one way of approach, for all people, whatever their background may be. The single law for native and foreigner in Numbers 15 was a shadow of this glorious truth. Whether we were near or far off, whether our fathers knew the covenants or were complete strangers to them, we all now come to God in exactly the same way, through the one sacrifice of Christ. There is not one gospel for one kind of person and another gospel for another kind.

There is one Human Saviour, one sacrifice, one pleasing aroma, and one open way to the Father for every willing heart. Let us therefore come near with gladness, knowing that we are accepted, not because of who we are or where we came from, but because of the one perfect offering to which all our worship is joined.

title: Prayer
text:
Our Father in Heaven,
We thank You that the offering of Christ was the truest pleasing aroma ever to rise before You.

Teach us that our character, our walk in the Spirit, and our surrender please You through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Guard us from ever thinking our own works could be accepted apart from His sacrifice.

We thank You that in Christ the wall between us has been broken down.

Near or far, we all now come to You by one sacrifice and one open way.

Christ loved us and offered himself as a sacrifice for us, a pleasing aroma to God. Ephesians 5:2

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
